Posted July 9, 2001
Analysis by Richard Cowan

More and more countries are seeking ways to reduce or eliminate the damage caused by cannabis prohibition.

Yesterday, David Blunkett, the UK Home Secretary (Justice Minister) called for an " adult, intelligent debate " on cannabis prohibition, which is a big improvement over the Blair government's previous refusal to even think about the laws.

In fact, cannabis prohibition is crumbing very rapidly there and Blunkett’s call for a debate is just recognizing that one is already raging. It is noteworthy that Blunkett still rejected the idea of a Royal Commission, but even the anti-prohibitionists tend to agree with him on that. The world needs a public debate, not just another elite hearing.
See
The Accelerating Disintegration of Marijuana Prohibition in Europe. If the Tories Are " all about sex, drugs and rock'n'roll, " Where Can the Left Go? Embarrassment for Swedes. Dutch PM for Dinner.

In Canada, both houses of parliament have committees studying the issues.
See
The Beginning of The End: Canadian Parliament Puts Marijuana Prohibition On Trial. Events in Switzerland and Other Countries Run Parallel Course. We Are Winning! Analysis By Richard Cowan

And in both countries there are significant court challenges to cannabis prohibition.
See
Extraordinary Editorial in Winnipeg Free Press Outlines " Findings of Fact " In Possession Case to Be Heard by Canadian Supreme Court.
and
As Court Challenges Mount to UK Cannabis Prohibition, London Times Op-ed By Retired Chief Constable Predicts -- " Human Rights Act will make cannabis legal. "

New Zealand is also holding hearings on the subject.
See
Debate Heats Up As New Zealand Begins to " Study " Cannabis Use. Perhaps They Should Also Study the Effects of Prohibition and the Dangers of the Therapeutic State. -- 2 Items.

So is Jamaica.
See
We Are Winning: Jamaica To Establish National Commission On Ganja; Dutch, Germans and Swiss to Hold Conference in the Spring.

The Swiss, who are accustomed to going their own way, are well along in the process.
See
We Are Winning! Switzerland to Surpass the Dutch and Allow Not Only Use and Sales – But Also Cultivation. Major Impact On Germany and the Rest of Europe.

Although each country has its own laws and its own reasons for questioning them and will arrive at its own conclusions, there are reasons why reformers -- and everyone who wants just and effective laws – should seek to add an international dimension to the debate on cannabis prohibition.

First, there is a need to learn from the experience of others. Most of these experiences will be negative, but that will at least keep others from making the same mistakes. The Dutch are no longer quite unique in having positive experiences.
See
We Are Winning! Switzerland to Surpass the Dutch and Allow Not Only Use and Sales – But Also Cultivation. Major Impact On Germany and the Rest of Europe.

But they also have some mistakes to learn from. The fact that they were largely the result foreign pressure does not mean that they were not mistakes.
See
Dutch Parliament Surprises Its Own Government -- Votes to " Legalize " Cultivation of Marijuana – By One Vote.

It has been very interesting to see the level of ignorance, even among UK politicians, who should know much more about the Dutch, so one should not assume that this is a problem unique to DEAland. Moreover, sharing of information internationally would embolden politicians who really do want to do the right thing.

Obviously, more knowledge is a good thing, but beyond the value in sharing information, and letting politicians know that this is the age of the Internet and " the world is watching, " there are other compelling reasons for internationalizing the debate.

First, DEAland has consistently interfered in the internal affairs of countries that deviate from International Prohibitionism, just as the late Soviets did for Communism. This is done both directly and through the UN.
See
Ottawa Citizen Columnist Dan Gardner Assails Canadian Justice Minister’s Kowtowing to UN and DEAland Narks: " U.S. says jump, we say how high? "
and
UN Narks At It Again, Attack Canada’s Punishment of Marijuana Growers As Only " A Slap on the Wrist. " Justice Minister Grovels. " Critics Dismiss UN Drug Report As US – Driven "
and
Today Is " International Anti-Drug Day " – Really. And Top UN Nark Wants To Censor Internet. Anti-Prohibitionism Equated With Genocide. The Internet Community Needs To Wake Up!
and links

Some small countries, such as Jamaica, are much more vulnerable to DEAland and UN pressure, but even Canadians tend to be unduly paranoid about their huge neighbor.

The cliché about there being strength in numbers certainly applies here. While DEAland may try to intimidate or pressure one country, it will be much more difficult to pressure several acting in concert. Moreover, DEAland’s international standing and influence has declined significantly recently.

See
We Really Are Winning! DEAland Loses Seat On UN Nark Committee; Europe Abandoning Cannabis Prohibition.
and links

But what about the various UN treaties that supposedly commit them to maintaining prohibition? Even though the Dutch have broken the spell and have begun talking about amending the treaties, the treaties have been used as excuses by prohibitionists and politicians in general – who have apparently never read them -- to avoid even discussing ways to end prohibition.
See
We Are Winning! The Dutch Government Shows More Confidence that Things Are Going Our Way in Europe.

The good news is that these treaties, as with everything else about cannabis prohibition, are largely frauds.

I say that these treaties are frauds because they are essentially pointless – and toothless. They are pointless, because they supposedly require their signatories to have laws that are of no international significance, that is, they involve things that should be of no consequence to other countries.

They are toothless because they have major loopholes and no enforcement mechanism.

First and foremost, all of them say in various ways that their requirements are " Subject to the constitutional limitations of a Party, its legal system and domestic law. " (from the 1961 Single Convention).

In other words, if the Canadian courts rule that cannabis prohibition is unconstitutional, the treaties’ requirements to punish Canadian citizens are null and void. Of course, the Dutch have proven for years that simply pretending that the law means what it says works fairly well.

Not only do the treaties lack any enforcement mechanisms -- that is DEAland cannot invade Canada to enforce " International Law " – they all have provisions for " Denunciation. " That is a diplomatic, not a moral term, even though the treaties should be " denounced " in a very undiplomatic way. In this context it simply means, " renounced " – as in opt out.

For example, Article 46 of the 1961 Single Convention, DENUNCIATION, says,

" 1. After the expiry of two years from the date of the coming into force of this Convention any Party may… denounce this Convention by an instrument in writing deposited with the Secretary-General.

2. The denunciation, if received by the Secretary-General on or before the first day of July in any year, shall take effect on the first day of January in the succeeding year, and, if received after the first day of July, shall take effect as if it had been received on or before the first day of July in the succeeding year. "

That’s it. Adios.
(For the full text of the 1961, 1971 and 1988 treaties see http://www.incb.org/e/conv )

If the Dutch and others decide to " denounce " the treaties because of their dissatisfaction, there is nothing that anyone can do about it, but of course this is something that they would prefer to do in concert with at least a few other countries. Needless to say, DEAland would ignore and/or denounce, one way or another, any treaty that no longer suits its purposes or pleases its politicians.
See
Bush Changes the Global Climate for Marijuana Prohibition. Analysis by Richard Cowan

All that is required to begin the global debate on cannabis prohibition is for the various national reform movements to coordinate their work over the Internet. More formal structures should be easy to create as the debates develop nationally. I am going to do what I can over the next few months to push the project. Ultimately, this will influence events in DEAland. It will certainly influence the elites and hasten the end of cannabis prohibition, even there.

Cannabis prohibition has become a global threat to freedom and its end can be hastened by reformers around the world joining together internationally, as is now easily possible – and as is now surely necessary.

Denunciation, anyone?
